Introductory Chemistry: Chemical Bonding and Reactions

Electronegativity is the tendency of an atom to attract shared electrons in a bond. Electronegativity increases across a period and decreases down a group, because atomic radius shrinks across a period and grows down a group.

An ionic bond forms when one atom transfers electrons to another, producing oppositely charged ions held together by electrostatic attraction. A covalent bond forms when two atoms share electrons instead. Ionic bonds differ from covalent bonds in that ionic compounds conduct electricity when molten, while most covalent compounds do not.

A catalyst is a substance that increases the rate of a reaction without being consumed. A catalyst works by providing an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, so a larger fraction of collisions has enough energy to react.

Le Chatelier's principle states that a system at equilibrium responds to a disturbance by shifting in the direction that partially offsets the change. Increasing the pressure on a gaseous equilibrium shifts the position toward the side with fewer moles of gas.

Oxidation is the loss of electrons and reduction is the gain of electrons. These processes always occur together, because the electrons lost by one species must be gained by another.

Activation energy is the minimum energy that colliding particles must possess for a reaction to occur. Raising the temperature increases the average kinetic energy of the particles, which increases the reaction rate.
